Zama-Zamas Go Legit

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Klipwal gold mine in KZN was at risk of losing control of their mine to Zama-Zamas. How did they manage to transform the battle into a business?

Unique Selling Point:
When people hear the words Zama-Zamas, it instills a sense of fear, lawlessness, within a secretive dog-eat-dog world of thuggery and gangsterism deep in the bowels of mines scattered across South Africa. Existence is treacherous for these illegal miners, living hand to mouth and in danger of losing their lives at any time, whilst venturing into the deep underground with no legitimacy or safety. Now one gold mine in KZN that was at risk of losing control of their mine to these Zama-Zamas, has transformed this battle into a business, by legitimising these so called subterranean gangsters into legal miners. An inspirational story, but still with some challenges.

Summary:
So how did Klipwal win this battle and is it a model for other mines to follow suit in South Africa?

Klipwal Mine is a relatively high grade mine with significant broken ore and un-mined areas that make it an attractive opportunity for its owners to re-equip the main shaft.

Due to the high levels of illegal mining it was decided to utilize the local illegal miners as the main workforce and keep the sophistication of mining at a very low level. This involves mining as it was many years ago – the men manually load ore into bags, it is raised from one level to the next via mono-winches, and then the bags are loaded onto coco-pans and pushed by hand to the adit (mine entrance).

The ex-illegals (Zama Zama’s) have been formed into legal entities called Co-ops (of 10 men each) and are remunerated on the basis of each ton lashed and trammed to a collection point. This method has had a profound effect in that it has made management and control relatively easy. The Co-ops are motivated and self-disciplined, and are contractors, not employees.

The mine provides full managerial and safety cover using permanent employees that are not induced to take ‘short cuts’, and has to comply with all DMRE regulations.
Management now plays a role of planning, leading, organizing and controlling as opposed to pressurizing employees and ultimately having to take disciplinary action.


Further information:
It’s a model on direct performance-based production with full time safety and managerial oversight as the way forward. These ex Zama Zamas are even covered for death by the mine as part of their insurance cover, so should anything happen to them their families have something to fall back on. This could never be the case as illegal miners. There are 159 of these cooperative members, and the payroll for the past 8 months varied between R700k to R950k per month, they work on a rotational basis so that different co-ops have turns at different levels, and when mining conditions are tough, they reduce their hours.

The Mine envisages that this system can be modified once they have re-equipped the shaft and are hoisting material in a more conventional fashion. They also believe that this system can be replicated at future mines they own and is very favourably viewed by DMRE, as a possible role model of dealing with the legacy of illegal mining across the country.
Currently the mine is also trying to engage the DMRE in considering the concept of Tribute mining which is used in countries like Zimbabwe, and works very well. This is where miners can lease parts of a mine legally from the mine owner, this principle does lessen the degree of illegal mining. At present, it is not legal in South Africa.

The mines need police assistance, but they seem uninterested in enforcing the law on these mines in KZN. CEO Richard Tait says, “this is the positive side of the story. The truth is that because the police are, incompetent, corrupt, or a combination thereof, we have to manage our own security. At times this has led to full-on confrontation and gun battles, and we have currently lost control of one area on our claim where the army will be needed. It is an interesting space!”

I have access to mine owners Richard Tait and Quintin George who is willing to speak, some of the co-op Zama-Zamas on how being given the opportunity to go legal has changed their lives, as well as one of the most notorious Illegal miners in the area, who is now a contractual consulting engineer for the mine, even though he doesn’t have an engineering degree. He knows the mine backwards, he grew up mining ore illegally but now he is not labeled a criminal.

POSSIBLE ADDITIONALS
There is a possibility that I may need an additional day shoot for an interview with the DMR in KZN if they are unable to meet us on the mine site when we are there. This could be done via zoom. If needs be another expert on artisenal mining Janet Munakamwe, although the mine owner himself is very familiar with all the pros and cons. This can be done without a presenter, so camera costs for that day with cameraman would be an additional R5 500,00. This may not be necessary, I will know closer to the time.

Press Release:


All over South Africa illegal miners risk their lives to eke out a meagre existence. One mine in KZN has persuaded some of these Zama Zamas to turn their backs on gangsterism and dangerous operations. Carte Blanche goes underground to witness a remarkable turnaround, where reformed Zama Zamas are now legal co-ops, excavating gold at Klipwal Mine.

Script:


VO: These men are known as Zama Zamas - illegal miners, descending into the bowels of mines scattered across South Africa. Lawless and desperate they know no fear.
Mduduzi: You know it's dangerous to be a zama zama, we're always taking high risk.
VO: Crumbling mine shafts, falling rock, rival gangs - they put their lives on the line - hoping for their pot of gold, but most often, they eke out a paltry existence with no legitimacy or safety.
Mduduzi: We were just hustling, because we didn't have a job, we didn't have work.
VO: Mduduzi Nyawo, lives in the Pongola region of KwaZulu Natal where unemployment and poverty is inescapable. Needing to support his family he resorted to illegal mining in the area, but the work underground was perilous, and the money erratic.

Mduduzi: We worked late at night only, because we're illegal. So you could wait even three days, just waiting for your chance. Then you’d get into the hole and you'll work if it's your turn.

VO: Faced with the possibility of injury and even death he was desperate for change - and then he was offered an opportunity that turned his life around.
//Beat music mountain walking
Link: Standing here on the hills of Northern Kwazulu Natal, bordering the Ithala Game Reserve one wouldn't think that just over there, the Klipwal Gold Mine is in full operation.
Quinton River: We've essentially got an 8000 Hectare mineral right. It's a long, old established mining property.
VO: When Bosveld Mines bought the mine in 2018, CEO Quinton George knew they were taking a chance.
LINK: Just a few years ago, the zama zamas had taken over, and it wasn't this peaceful.
Quinton River: Every day, every week, every month, we’re arresting people trying to stop it. It was quite aggressive.
Mac: What was happening?
Quinton River: Put it this way, lives were lost. I mean, at one point, we had an attack on the mine, equipment was burned. Some of our staff were injured, And there was a time we thought we actually would lose the mine.
VO: They came up with a bold plan - to transform the zama zamas into formalized co-operatives of artisanal miners. // But first they would need them to buy into the idea.
Mduduzi: We didn't easily agree to it, but some people did want it, just like me, I wanted it, because I could see that we are unsafe there, we’re taking risk every day, the injuries were high, even fatalities down there.
Quinton River: We managed to eventually get enough people co-opted, that were illegal miners. They had PPE, they were inducted and trained by us and converted them from hostile zama zamas into teams of people that worked on our side.

VO: Of the mine's 400 workers, about 170 of them belong to these co-ops and we're venturing underground with them this morning, to the heartbeat of the mine.
Quinton: Most of the deposit is underneath the mountain*we're able to drive down the side to sixth level, which is 200 metres below where we are here.
VO: Getting suited up, it struck me how crucial safety is, under the co-op system, these artisanals are now covered for injury and death, which they never were before. The hazardous blasting and drilling are done by the mine's trained staff, while the co-ops do the heavy lifting.
Elvis: Before we were zama zamas, but then I started working here
Mac: Here in the mine?
Elvis: Ja, subcontracting to this company.
VO: Elvis Mavuso is a co-op team leader, and has already been underground since 6 am.
Mac: How many co-ops are there here?
Elvis: Co-ops, around 17, but we go in groups of 10 per team.
Mac: So what targets are you pushing for?
Elvis: Most of the time we aim for 16 tons, 17 per day, Maybe if we push we stop at 20, there the money looks better.
Mac: (eng) And they pay you according to how much you take out?
Elvis: Ja
VO: Bags of rock emerge from the deep, winched along this traffic way.
SU Mac: All of these bags that come here, they carry gold?
VO: The mine operates 24/7 and the co-ops work in shifts digging and loading on levels way below. As it is, it's pretty dangerous.
Link: One can't even imagine what it must be like here as a Zama zama. No lights, no safety, not knowing whether the shaft has been secured or not, and not knowing even if you're going to get anything from the ore. So what Klipwal mine has managed to do here is absolutely incredible.
Mac: How has it helped you as a person working for the mine in a co-op.
Elvis: Eish, it's the fact that I can support my family
Link: So the model is very simple. You take these zama zamas, and you make them a part of the value chain of the mine, you incentivize them for the hard work that they do, then you've got a happy community and a safer mine.
SU Mac: Two tons, I just pushed two tons.. UH!
VO: At Klipwal there is a glimmer of hope for a community that's living hand to mouth. But just a short drive away at Bosveld’s Kortnek mine, the tension is palpable.
Quinton: We're not going to go the whole way. Because we're not sure it's safe. We're not sure what condition the road’s in.
VO: Here lives have been lost in rock falls and hostile night attacks. George and his security detail survey the area.
SU Quinton: Those are the spotters… 2 ja
Link: You could say this is a tale of two mines; one where a war was fought and won by Bosveld mines, and here just 10 kilometres away, in Kortnek where it's become the Wild Wild West.
Quinton Kortnek: We had about 40 people that were working here and with COVID we had to close it. The artisanals have moved in, you can see them living under the trees. They've got the little gas bottles as mills and they're using mercury and there's anything from 50 to 150 at one point in time.
Mac: Where do these people come from ?
Quinton Kortnek: So, a number of locals it’s guys from Mozambique, from Swaziland, there's women, there's children that are working.
VO: Situated Twenty kilometres from the Eswatini border, it's remote, with no communications and no power.
Quinton Kortnek: Even the police when they come here it's very hard for them to have the right vehicles, have the right manpower and even if you clear it out once by the time they leave, more people come back in.
VO: Always vigilant, when the Zama Zamas spot our drone they let us know we aren't welcome.
Quinton Kortnek: I just think you're never going to solve it, fighting it. So there's got to be some sort of cooperative incentive and working together, it has to be the solution.
VO: Klipwal Mine is the largest single source of work for the local community, so one would imagine the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy would take a keen interest in supporting the mine.
VO: when we asked the DMRE for its perspective on Klipwal's co-op model, they failed to respond.
//BEAT Music change
VO: But the solutions for illegal mining are complex, especially on the Witwatersrand Gold Reef where migrant labour issues are amplified, according to Dr Janet Munakamwe of the Wits Mining Institute.

Janet: There is war all the time within that particular sector. So I guess also supporting the zama zamas, contributes positively to the economy of South Africa

VO: As a labour migration policy specialist, she has interviewed many Zama Zamas and gained insight into their plight.
In 2017 she made recommendations to the DMRE to include zama zamas in their artisanal mining framework, but there's been very little traction for her policy proposition.
Janet: Part of my empirical evidence pointed to the need for big mining companies to support zama zamas as a win-win situation in which some of the problems, like for instance, the trespassing issues, are mitigated. At the same time, also zama zamas will be benefiting from in terms of health and safety,
VO: Munakamwe believes the Bosveld Mines’ model could be adapted for the Witwatersrand, much like Zimbabwe where artisanal mining has started contributing to the country’s revenue.
Janet: But it only started happening after they'd formalised artisanal mining through tributa4ry mining whereby the big mines had to support the small-scale miners.
VO: For now Bosveld mines is going it alone, teetering between policy and survival.
Quinton Kortnek: Once we've got enough economic activity and jobs, the community kind of become your policemen as well, because they'll protect their economic interests, and before you know, the illegal activity stops, they disappear
VO: But in this terrain uncertainty is ever-present. Back in Klipwal near the river, the road is blockaded - a new band of Zama Zamas is claiming their turf.
Quinton River: Eight weeks ago, there was a discovery of a reasonably nice attractive vein. And within a week and a half, some illegal activity had already moved in, the guys threatened our staff, they threatened our samplers.
Mac: Have you tried to engage with them?
Quinton River: I think we're very close to a point where they'll come to us and say they need our help, or can they get jobs?

VO: The prospect of a steady income is what motivated Mduduzi Nyawo to turn his back on illegal mining and become a co-op leader.
Mduduzi: Some of us have even got promotions, just like me.
Mac: Oh, you got promoted?
Mduduzi: I got promoted. you see, now that I'm working in the lamp room, I'm working permanently now.
Mac: That's great! ( or Dude!! or My guy!!?)
Mduduzi: You know, I have wife three children.
Mac: Are they happy that you're now working here as opposed to being a zama zama.
Mduduzi At least now I have a payslip, I can open any credit, you know.

VO: Looking to the future, Nyawo's children may benefit from Quinton George's dream - to invest in conservation and ecotourism, creating jobs long after the mine is gone. But much has to go right for that to become a reality.

VO: Elvis Mavuso is a co-op team leader, and has already been underground since 6 am. Mac: How many co-ops are there here? Elvis: Co-ops, around 17, but we go in groups of 10 per team. Mac: So what targets are you pushing for? Elvis: Most of the time we aim for 16 tons, 17 per day, Maybe if we push we stop at 20, there the money looks better. Mac: (eng) And they pay you according to how much you take out? Elvis: Ja VO: Bags of rock emerge from the deep, winched along this traffic way. SU Mac: All of these bags that come here, they carry gold? VO: The mine operates 24/7 and the co-ops work in shifts digging and loading on levels way below. As it is, it's pretty dangerous. Link: One can't even imagine what it must be like here as a Zama zama. No lights, no safety, not knowing whether the shaft has been secured or not, and not knowing even if you're going to get anything from the ore. So what Klipwal mine has managed to do here is absolutely incredible. Mac: How has it helped you as a person working for the mine in a co-op. Elvis: Eish, it's the fact that I can support my family Link: So the model is very simple. You take these zama zamas, and you make them a part of the value chain of the mine, you incentivize them for the hard work that they do, then you've got a happy community and a safer mine. SU Mac: Two tons, I just pushed two tons.. UH! VO: At Klipwal there is a glimmer of hope for a community that's living hand to mouth. But just a short drive away at Bosveld’s Kortnek mine, the tension is palpable. Quinton: We're not going to go the whole way. Because we're not sure it's safe. We're not sure what condition the road’s in. VO: Here lives have been lost in rock falls and hostile night attacks. George and his security detail survey the area. SU Quinton: Those are the spotters… 2 ja Link: You could say this is a tale of two mines; one where a war was fought and won by Bosveld mines, and here just 10 kilometres away, in Kortnek where it's become the Wild Wild West. Quinton Kortnek: We had about 40 people that were working here and with COVID we had to close it. The artisanals have moved in, you can see them living under the trees. They've got the little gas bottles as mills and they're using mercury and there's anything from 50 to 150 at one point in time. Mac: Where do these people come from ? Quinton Kortnek: So, a number of locals it’s guys from Mozambique, from Swaziland, there's women, there's children that are working. VO: Situated Twenty kilometres from the Eswatini border, it's remote, with no communications and no power. Quinton Kortnek: Even the police when they come here it's very hard for them to have the right vehicles, have the right manpower and even if you clear it out once by the time they leave, more people come back in. VO: Always vigilant, when the Zama Zamas spot our drone they let us know we aren't welcome. Quinton Kortnek: I just think you're never going to solve it, fighting it. So there's got to be some sort of cooperative incentive and working together, it has to be the solution. VO: Klipwal Mine is the largest single source of work for the local community, so one would imagine the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy would take a keen interest in supporting the mine. VO: when we asked the DMRE for its perspective on Klipwal's co-op model, they failed to respond. //BEAT Music change VO: But the solutions for illegal mining are complex, especially on the Witwatersrand Gold Reef where migrant labour issues are amplified, according to Dr Janet Munakamwe of the Wits Mining Institute. Janet: There is war all the time within that particular sector. So I guess also supporting the zama zamas, contributes positively to the economy of South Africa VO: As a labour migration policy specialist, she has interviewed many Zama Zamas and gained insight into their plight. In 2017 she made recommendations to the DMRE to include zama zamas in their artisanal mining framework, but there's been very little traction for her policy proposition. Janet: Part of my empirical evidence pointed to the need for big mining companies to support zama zamas as a win-win situation in which some of the problems, like for instance, the trespassing issues, are mitigated. At the same time, also zama zamas will be benefiting from in terms of health and safety, VO: Munakamwe believes the Bosveld Mines’ model could be adapted for the Witwatersrand, much like Zimbabwe where artisanal mining has started contributing to the country’s revenue. Janet: But it only started happening after they'd formalised artisanal mining through tributa4ry mining whereby the big mines had to support the small-scale miners. VO: For now Bosveld mines is going it alone, teetering between policy and survival. Quinton Kortnek: Once we've got enough economic activity and jobs, the community kind of become your policemen as well, because they'll protect their economic interests, and before you know, the illegal activity stops, they disappear VO: But in this terrain uncertainty is ever-present. Back in Klipwal near the river, the road is blockaded - a new band of Zama Zamas is claiming their turf. Quinton River: Eight weeks ago, there was a discovery of a reasonably nice attractive vein. And within a week and a half, some illegal activity had already moved in, the guys threatened our staff, they threatened our samplers. Mac: Have you tried to engage with them? Quinton River: I think we're very close to a point where they'll come to us and say they need our help, or can they get jobs? VO: The prospect of a steady income is what motivated Mduduzi Nyawo to turn his back on illegal mining and become a co-op leader. Mduduzi: Some of us have even got promotions, just like me. Mac: Oh, you got promoted? Mduduzi: I got promoted. you see, now that I'm working in the lamp room, I'm working permanently now. Mac: That's great! ( or Dude!! or My guy!!?) Mduduzi: You know, I have wife three children. Mac: Are they happy that you're now working here as opposed to being a zama zama. Mduduzi At least now I have a payslip, I can open any credit, you know. VO: Looking to the future, Nyawo's children may benefit from Quinton George's dream - to invest in conservation and ecotourism, creating jobs long after the mine is gone. But much has to go right for that to become a reality.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Klipwal gold mine in KZN was at risk of losing control of their mine to Zama-Zamas. How did they manage to transform the battle into a business?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: When people hear the words Zama-Zamas, it instills a sense of fear, lawlessness, within a secretive dog-eat-dog world of thuggery and gangsterism deep in the bowels of mines scattered across South Africa. Existence is treacherous for these illegal miners, living hand to mouth and in danger of losing their lives at any time, whilst venturing into the deep underground with no legitimacy or safety. Now one gold mine in KZN that was at risk of losing control of their mine to these Zama-Zamas, has transformed this battle into a business, by legitimising these so called subterranean gangsters into legal miners. An inspirational story, but still with some challenges.
metadata.Summary: So how did Klipwal win this battle and is it a model for other mines to follow suit in South Africa? Klipwal Mine is a relatively high grade mine with significant broken ore and un-mined areas that make it an attractive opportunity for its owners to re-equip the main shaft. Due to the high levels of illegal mining it was decided to utilize the local illegal miners as the main workforce and keep the sophistication of mining at a very low level. This involves mining as it was many years ago – the men manually load ore into bags, it is raised from one level to the next via mono-winches, and then the bags are loaded onto coco-pans and pushed by hand to the adit (mine entrance). The ex-illegals (Zama Zama’s) have been formed into legal entities called Co-ops (of 10 men each) and are remunerated on the basis of each ton lashed and trammed to a collection point. This method has had a profound effect in that it has made management and control relatively easy. The Co-ops are motivated and self-disciplined, and are contractors, not employees. The mine provides full managerial and safety cover using permanent employees that are not induced to take ‘short cuts’, and has to comply with all DMRE regulations. Management now plays a role of planning, leading, organizing and controlling as opposed to pressurizing employees and ultimately having to take disciplinary action.
metadata.Further information: It’s a model on direct performance-based production with full time safety and managerial oversight as the way forward. These ex Zama Zamas are even covered for death by the mine as part of their insurance cover, so should anything happen to them their families have something to fall back on. This could never be the case as illegal miners. There are 159 of these cooperative members, and the payroll for the past 8 months varied between R700k to R950k per month, they work on a rotational basis so that different co-ops have turns at different levels, and when mining conditions are tough, they reduce their hours. The Mine envisages that this system can be modified once they have re-equipped the shaft and are hoisting material in a more conventional fashion. They also believe that this system can be replicated at future mines they own and is very favourably viewed by DMRE, as a possible role model of dealing with the legacy of illegal mining across the country. Currently the mine is also trying to engage the DMRE in considering the concept of Tribute mining which is used in countries like Zimbabwe, and works very well. This is where miners can lease parts of a mine legally from the mine owner, this principle does lessen the degree of illegal mining. At present, it is not legal in South Africa. The mines need police assistance, but they seem uninterested in enforcing the law on these mines in KZN. CEO Richard Tait says, “this is the positive side of the story. The truth is that because the police are, incompetent, corrupt, or a combination thereof, we have to manage our own security. At times this has led to full-on confrontation and gun battles, and we have currently lost control of one area on our claim where the army will be needed. It is an interesting space!” I have access to mine owners Richard Tait and Quintin George who is willing to speak, some of the co-op Zama-Zamas on how being given the opportunity to go legal has changed their lives, as well as one of the most notorious Illegal miners in the area, who is now a contractual consulting engineer for the mine, even though he doesn’t have an engineering degree. He knows the mine backwards, he grew up mining ore illegally but now he is not labeled a criminal.
